Singing of Psalms
SING-ing uv SAHMZ
noun phrase
From Old English singan (to sing, to make music with the voice) and Latin psalmus (a sacred song, from Greek psalmos, a song sung to a stringed instrument, from psallein, to pluck a string). The practice of singing the biblical Psalter as the church's primary hymn book is as old as synagogue worship and was carried into the New Testament church; the Reformation rediscovered it as the norm of Reformed corporate praise.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The singing of psalms is the corporate worship practice of setting the 150 canonical Psalms to music and singing them as the covenant community's primary or exclusive vehicle of praise. Paul commands the Colossians to let “the word of Christ dwell in” them richly, “teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God” (Col. 3:16). The Ephesians passage parallels this (Eph. 5:19). The word “psalms” in both texts points to the biblical Psalter; “hymns” and “spiritual songs” are plausibly understood as further descriptions of Psalm categories rather than distinct classes of uninspired hymns.

The Psalter is the church's divinely inspired hymnbook: 150 Spirit-breathed songs covering the full range of the covenant life — lament (Ps. 22), penitence (Ps. 51), praise (Ps. 150), imprecation (Ps. 109), confidence (Ps. 23), and eschatological longing (Ps. 72). Exclusive psalmody holds that the Regulative Principle requires singing only what Scripture has prescribed — the Psalter — and that uninspired human compositions are not warranted for corporate worship. Those in the Reformed tradition who allow hymns alongside the Psalms (the majority position in mainstream Reformed churches) nonetheless insist that the Psalter must hold the primary place and that the imprecatory psalms, psalms of lament, and psalms of conquest must not be suppressed. The Genevan Psalter (1562) and the Scottish Psalter (1650) stand as the great monuments of the Reformed singing tradition.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined psalm as “a sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject, and in honor of God.” The singing of the biblical Psalms was, for Webster as for the Reformers, the normative mode of corporate praise.

expand to see more

PSALM, n. [L. psalmus; Gr. psalmos, from psallo, to sing, or to touch or strike a stringed instrument; to play.]

A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject, and in honor of God. The Psalms of David, in the Old Testament, comprise 150 sacred poems, and are the inspired hymn-book of the Jewish and Christian church.

The Book of Psalms is the longest book in the Bible, and was the standard hymn-book of both the synagogue and the early Christian church, though in later centuries the church supplemented and in some traditions largely replaced it with uninspired compositions.

SINGING, ppr. [from sing.] Uttering sounds with musical modulations of voice. In worship, the offering of praise and prayer to God through the vehicle of metrical song, whether accompanied or unaccompanied by instruments.

The singing of psalms in the Reformation tradition signifies the recovery of the Psalter as the primary or exclusive vehicle of corporate praise, set in metrical versions (Genevan, Scottish) so that the whole congregation could participate.

Key Scripture

Col. 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom — teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs — singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God."

Eph. 5:19 — "speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs — singing and making melody with your heart to the Lord;"

Ps. 95:2 — "Let us come before His presence with thanksgiving; let us shout joyfully to Him with psalms."

Ps. 100:2 — "Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing."

Modern Corruption

Modern evangelical worship has largely displaced the Psalter with commercially produced praise music that reflects contemporary sentimentalism rather than the full covenantal range of Spirit-inspired praise.

expand to see more

The most consequential corruption in modern evangelical worship is the wholesale displacement of the Psalter by Contemporary Christian Music (CCM), praise choruses, and commercially produced worship songs. These songs are characteristically horizontal (addressed to the congregation about feelings rather than to God), theologically thin, repetitive in structure, and largely absent of lament, imprecation, or the full range of biblical emotion. The result is a church that has lost the capacity to sing its own sorrow, its own repentance, its own cry for vengeance on the wicked, and its own longing for the day of Christ — because its hymnody has been stripped of every Psalm that makes the contemporary worshiper uncomfortable. This is not a liturgical preference question; it is a discipleship catastrophe.

Within the Reformed tradition itself, the debate over exclusive psalmody versus the allowance of uninspired hymns alongside the Psalter has produced a secondary corruption: the complete neglect of the Psalter in churches that have, in theory, not rejected it. Churches that claim to allow both Psalms and hymns in practice sing almost no Psalms at all — reducing the Psalter to an occasional liturgical ornament rather than the church's living hymnbook. The corrective is not merely the recovery of psalmody in principle but its practice: sung Psalms every Lord's Day, in metrical versions that the congregation can memorize and carry out of the sanctuary into the week.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word psalm traces from Hebrew through Greek to the practice of singing sacred poetry to stringed accompaniment — the Psalter being the divinely inspired collection that has defined covenant worship across the ages.

expand to see more

Hebrew mizmor (מִזמוֹר) — a melody, a song sung to string accompaniment; the word that heads 57 of the 150 Psalms in the Hebrew Psalter, indicating the primary mode of performance as sung music

Greek psallein (ψάλλειν) — to pluck a string, to make music on a stringed instrument; extended in the Septuagint to the singing of Psalms; the verb from which psalmos and psaltery derive

Greek psalmos (ψαλμόσ) — a song sung to a stringed instrument; used in the Septuagint to translate the Hebrew mizmor; the standard New Testament word for the canonical Psalms of David

Latin psalmus — adopted into the Vulgate from the Greek; entering all Western European languages as the standard word for the sacred songs of the Psalter, carried into English as psalm

Middle English psalm (c. 1300) — entering English through the Old French psalme and Latin psalmus; the word has always carried the specific sense of the canonical Davidic songs rather than religious song generically

Usage

"Calvin's Genevan Psalter (1562), with its metrical Psalms set to melodies by Louis Bourgeois, was designed to put the Word of God on the lips of the entire congregation — a liturgical revolution that made the gathered people active singers of Scripture rather than passive listeners to a trained choir."

"The Scottish Psalter of 1650 remains in use in Free Presbyterian and Reformed Presbyterian congregations today, a living testimony that the 150 Psalms are sufficient to carry the full weight of the church's praise across four centuries and every circumstance of life."

"Thomas Manton preached that “the Psalms are the best prayers and the best praises that ever were penned” — a commendation that rests on the Psalter's divine authorship and its capacity to express every state of the covenant soul before God."
